docs.title: GameStart
docs.text:
Welcome! GameStart is a cozy first-person tidy-up game set in a late-90s/2000s video-game store. You're the overnight clerk: the whole shop starts out in a glorious mess, and box by box you put it back in order — game boxes on the right shelves, consoles on their stands, merch where merch belongs. No timers, no customers, no pressure. Just you, the hum of the CRT at the counter, and a store that slowly becomes yours.

The twist: if you choose to connect your Steam profile, the games on the shelves are your own library — your actual games appear as physical boxes you can pick up, flip over, and shelve. (Totally optional — there's a built-in fictional catalog too. See Privacy.)

Heads up: GameStart is in development and not yet released. This wiki describes the current development build. Anything marked Planned is design intent and may change before release.

docs.text: This page is developer/modder-facing. It is the only wiki page allowed to use internal names — everywhere else the wiki speaks strictly in player terms (that rule is machine-checked by tools/wiki-term-lint/). If you're a player, you want the Glossary.

docs.title: Where the real documentation lives
docs.text:
• Design source of truth: gamestart-unity/Docs/README.md (reading order) — v2 spec + v4 finite-night spec + Brand Bible.
  • Pack format (modding): gamestart-unity/Docs/Design/GameStart_Curation_Packs.md.

  • Wiki editing rules & update workflow: wiki/_Maintenance.md.

Quiz gameplay is retired in both systems. Legacy quiz DTOs, wire frames, frozen world allocations and historical reward claims remain compatibility data. Retired physical quiz allocations remain normal unordered physical homes; the cut does not delete supported-save items or invent reward refunds.

The completion report snapshots GsStoreTidyingSnapshot: live WHITE copy progress minus the baseline, plus unique canonical titles whose required copies are all WHITE across variants. Later movement changes live HUD/save progress only. Finale presentation uses local phase state; independently skipping credits does not mutate the replicated progression hash.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Is the game out? Not yet — GameStart is in development. This wiki tracks the development build; pages mark in-development features as Planned.

What platforms? PC first (the game is built and tested for desktop). Anything beyond that is unannounced.

Do I need a Steam account to play? No. Connecting your Steam profile is optional — without it you get a full store of original fictional games. See Privacy.

Does my Steam data get uploaded anywhere? The optional library connection is read-only. Limited library details pass through GameStart's library service and can be held there temporarily. Privacy explains consent, local caching and what the service receives.

Is there co-op? Use CO-OP on Title to Host Game, join a friend's listed store, or enter a Session code. Regular New Game and Continue start solo stores. Hosting uses the selected save; the host saves the shared store, while guests keep their own local save slots separate.

In the pause menu's Co-op tab, the host can choose Private or Friends Only. Private stops new joins and hides the session code, Copy and Invite controls; friends already in the room stay connected. Friends Only makes those sharing controls available. Guests can see the roster and available code but cannot change privacy.

A failed join keeps the entered code, region and save selection for an explicit Retry. If an active session unexpectedly ends, you return to Title with a brief notice. Nothing automatically reconnects or claims that unsaved progress was saved.

Is there a timer or fail state? No. No customers, no shifts to survive, no clock pressure — time of day is ambiance. You can take your time. Picking games back up can reduce the current tidying count.

Can I rebind controls? Yes, fully — keyboard/mouse and gamepad. See Getting Started for defaults.

I get motion sick in first-person games. The settings' ACCESSIBILITY tab has a motion comfort section: one Reduce camera motion switch that calms everything at once, plus individual controls — a field of view slider, a head bob strength slider (zero turns it off), and toggles for the sprint FOV change and the landing camera dip. The GRAPHICS tab has resolution, refresh rate, and fullscreen controls, plus a frame limit option (VSync by default) that stops screen tearing. The camera also stays steady on its own when you walk up stairs, ramps, and piles of games.

Can I mod it? Yes — content packs can restock the store with custom fictional games, managed from an in-game screen. See Modding.

The last box — will I be hunting one lost item forever? The design explicitly guards against the "399 of 400" problem with tools already in the build: finished shelves keep a lit "done" gleam so what's left stands out, the Stock Sense glow outlines nearby copies of the game you're holding, and Tendril Grab reels those strays in from across your district — straight into your hands. See Talents & Gear.

Can I lose my save? If a save is damaged or cannot be loaded by the current version, the title screen offers Back up & start new game. It must back up the selected save before a new night starts; a backup failure keeps the form open and starts no game. See Getting Started.

docs.title: Controls (keyboard & mouse, and gamepad)
docs.text:
Every keyboard control can be rebound in the settings — this is the default layout. Where a gamepad button is listed it comes after the slash.

Action Default Move W A S D / Left stick Look Mouse / Right stick Switch between first- and third-person view (hold to look around your character) Left Ctrl / R3 Pick up / interact E or Left Click / A Launch an eligible game from its INFONET details page Click Launch or press L Launch an eligible game from the Pip-Boy readout Press L Put down / throw Q or Right Click (hold and release to throw) / RT Cycle through what you're holding Scroll wheel, or tap R / LB RB Inspect the held box (look closer) Hold F / Y Open / close the game's case while inspecting Left Click (while holding F) Zoom in for a closer look Hold C / LT Check the store map Hold Tab / Select Take every copy off the shelf slot you're aiming at T Open or close Base Stats B / D-pad Up Ping a spot for your co-op crew (aim at a player to ask "what/where?") Middle Click Open the emote wheel — pick an expression for your co-op crew Hold ` (backtick) Talk to your co-op crew (voice mode set to push to talk) Hold V / LB Cast a skill (see Talents & Gear) 1 2 3 4 5 6 Jump Space / B (tap or hold when charged jumping is enabled) Sprint (hold to run) Left Shift / L3 Crouch Z Pause Esc / Start

When you launch one of your own games this way, GameStart steps aside: it goes quiet, stops drawing the store, and waits in the background while the other game runs — your co-op session stays live the whole time. On Windows it also minimizes itself; on other platforms the window stays open and simply sits dark and silent. Come back to the GameStart window and everything picks up right where you left off.

A thrown box goes where you are looking: aim up to lob it over something, aim at the floor to bounce it down in front of you. The longer you hold Right Click, the harder it flies — and the faster it spins flat like a frisbee on the way. A quick click still just tosses it gently at your feet, no spin.

While you hold a throw, the box in your hands starts to shake, and shakes faster the longer you hold — that rattle is your wind-up gauge, so you can judge the throw without looking away from where you're aiming. It settles the moment you let go, cancel, or pause.

Where charged jumping is enabled, tap for the shortest jump, release partway for a higher jump, or charge fully and release for the highest jump. If automatic jumping is enabled, reaching full charge jumps immediately. A green bar appears below the crosshair only while the jump is charging.

Gamepad is supported with equivalent bindings — except the skill keys 1–6, which are keyboard-only for now. While the Portal Pistol skill is waiting for you to aim (after pressing 6), Left Click places the portal and Right Click cancels — your usual pick-up and put-down come back as soon as the pistol is done or cancelled. Settings has a toggle-to-run option for Sprint, so you don't have to hold the key down. The settings' ACCESSIBILITY tab collects the motion comfort options — field of view, head bob strength, and a Reduce camera motion switch that calms the camera in one press. The GRAPHICS tab has resolution, refresh rate, fullscreen, and a frame limit (VSync by default). A display-mode change previews for 15 seconds: choose Keep to save it or Revert to return to the previous mode. Cancel, closing the panel or waiting out the countdown also reverts. Other settings save when changed. The GENERAL tab carries the Language dropdown — Auto (Steam / system), English, 日本語, 简体中文, 繁體中文, 繁體中文（香港）, Deutsch, Français, Português (Brasil), 한국어, Español, or Español (Latinoamérica); Auto follows your Steam language for this game, then your system language. The GENERAL tab holds your player name and privacy. A new language applies to screens as they open, and box art keeps its printed language, the way an import shop's shelves would. GENERAL also has a switch that shows each game's genre beside its name in the bottom-right list of what you're holding — it starts off, and you can turn it on.

docs.title: Your first night
docs.text:
Pick NEW GAME, select a save slot, and choose your catalog: DEFAULT (the shipped mix), ALL PARODY (parody games only), or MY GAMES + SHIPPED if you've imported your Steam library. Choosing a catalog does not start the game; press START GAME when ready. An occupied slot asks you to confirm its backup before starting. The loading screen shows the current preparation stage and the actual number of game cases prepared. The very first night can take a few minutes while cover art is prepared; later nights are much faster. When it finishes, you're in.

  1. Look around. The store opens in "arranged chaos" — games and merch piled on counters, fixtures, and the floor. Everything loose has a home somewhere.
  2. Pick things up (E / Left Click). You can carry a small stack at once — the panel in the bottom-right names the game "in hand" (next to place) in big type, with your carry count out of the max stack (like 3 / 8) under it, and the rest of your pile queued above it — the line just above the big name is what comes out next. Scroll to flip through the stack and the queue reorders with it. The pile you're carrying drifts with your gaze: look up and it settles low so you can see past it, look down and it rides up out of the way — you keep an edge of it in sight either way, and the panel always tells you exactly what you're holding.
  3. Find the right spot. Hold a box near a shelf and a ghost preview shows where it would land. Once you've learned the Stock Sense skill, matching games glow to help you spot where the rest of the stack lives.
  4. Place it. If the spot is right, you get a satisfying chime and XP. If the box is in the wrong section, the shelf's price tag turns red — see Tidying & Price Tags.
  5. Check the terminal. The CRT computer at the counter is the store's brain: look up any game, see your play stats, and browse store info.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text:
The game saves when you pause. Return to Title is one action: in a solo store, a failed save keeps the store open so you can retry. In co-op, the host attempts to save before leaving; if that fails, the session still ends and Title reports the failure. Guests do not replace their own saves with the host's store.

LOAD GAME shows three save slots. Selecting a card previews that save; CONTINUE starts it. The main Title CONTINUE button resumes the selected save directly. An occupied card shows its current Completion percentage and Last played time. A save that did not record that progress shows Unavailable. An empty card offers New Game without invented progress.

Before a new game replaces an occupied slot, choose Cancel or Back up & start new game. Cancel keeps your slot and catalog choice. The backup covers only the selected slot; the other slots stay intact. If backup fails, no new game starts and the form stays available. No files are deleted by that backup operation.

If a save cannot be continued, its preview explains the problem and offers the same backup-and-new-game route. A temporary check failure can be retried; version or missing-content problems need the matching game version or content. This does not repair the old save.

You can Continue a completed save to visit the store, move items and use skills. The ending does not replay automatically. The host can deliberately use the OPEN sign to replay the credits; finishing or skipping that replay returns to Title. The original completion report and time stay unchanged.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
The player's dictionary — every term here is something you can see or do in the game. (Developers/modders: the technical mapping lives in the Dev Glossary.)

Term Meaning After-Hours Co-op The title screen's early co-op mode — host a session, share the co-op code, and a friend joins your store. The host saves the shared store; guests do not overwrite their own save slots Bubble Carry Active skill (key 5) — seals your held box in a bubble that floats it to its home shelf on its own; if that home is full, the bubble tries the next home for the same game, and pops nearby only when every home is full Portal Return Signature skill that sets a return pad at your feet and links it to a shelf slot you aim at, so boxes set down on the pad zip there (not on the default skill bar right now) Catalog choice The question every NEW GAME asks — what stocks the store tonight: DEFAULT, ALL PARODY, or MY GAMES + SHIPPED (only with a Steam import) Co-op code The short code a host shares so a friend can join their After-Hours Co-op session Deluxe Cart Passive skill — carry more boxes at once (two levels) Fictional catalog The store's built-in roster of original parody games, used when Steam isn't connected Gear The store gadgets your skills come from — see Talents & Gear Ghost preview The translucent outline showing where a held item would land Grand opening The store's completion event, started deliberately with the OPEN sign once its required homes are filled. The report records the original result; the first credit roll returns to that report, while a later replay returns to Title Plumbob Guide Passive skill — while you hold a box, a hovering gem marks the shelf where it belongs INFONET The store's information network — the counter terminal and Pip-Boy use it to show game details Inspect Holding F to bring the held box up close and read it Load order The #1, #2… order packs apply in — later packs win conflicts OPEN sign The sign by the front door. It reads CLOSED while the store still needs tidying; once the store is ready you can flip it to OPEN, which records the grand opening. A completed store can be visited again with Continue; the host can deliberately replay its credits through this sign. In After-Hours Co-op only the host can flip it — the sign tells everyone else so — and when the host does, every player in the session gets the same grand opening Platform families The four game registers, each with its own box style: PayStation (blue), Newtondo (red), XRocks (green), and Vapor (black, the PC platform by Spout). Every family owns a grouped shelving district — PayStation west, Newtondo south, Vapor north-west, XRocks north-east — each continuing onto the mezzanine deck Pack A folder of custom content that restocks the store (Modding) Price tag The tag on a shelf rail under each run of games: white = right home and every copy of that game is on this shelf; plain = right home but not every copy is here yet (or this shelf cannot hold every copy); yellow border = that game has a stack smaller than the night's planned copies-per-stack, or extra stacks beyond the night's plan, or a home elsewhere — every tag of that game wears it, finished white ones included; red = wrong section Tendril Grab Active skill (key 4) — reels copies of the game you're holding in from across your district, shelf fronts and loose strays alike, straight into your hands; later levels reach the neighbouring districts, dig behind the front copy, and finally pull from anywhere in the store, the whole catch at once Scope Shot Active skill (key 2) — scope in on the game you're holding, then place it into a distant empty slot with one shot, or send it flying if you miss Spotter Visor Retired from the tool bar. It used to light up every loose copy of the game you're holding nearby; Scope Shot has key 2 now Section A themed area of the store (platform districts, free shelves, counter, merch) with its own overhead sign Mezzanine The store's upper deck, reached by two ramps — platform districts continue upstairs Section sign / plaque The overhead sign naming a section; (Planned) lights up when the section is fully tidied Shelf Guide Active skill (key 1) — lights up the spot where your held box belongs for a short time Store map The two-floor map of the store — hold Tab to raise your own paper copy; the same map hangs by the front door and stands on the directory Store directory The reading stand just inside the entrance carrying the store map You are here The red diamond on the store map marking your position; its notch points the way you're facing Hold Piece Signature skill that swaps the box in your hands with the front copy of a stocked shelf slot (not on the default Tool bar right now) Skills The pause-menu tab where talent points buy and upgrade skills; the active ones cast with keys 1–6 Staff-pick badge (Planned) The fuzzy "how much was this played?" hint on a box's back — deliberately never exact numbers Stock Sense Passive skill — while you hold a box, nearby copies of the same game get a purple outline Pip-Boy Active skill (key 3) — opens an INFONET readout for the box you're holding; press 3 or Esc to close it. An owned, installed Steam game's readout can also launch it (L) Portal Pistol Active skill (key 6) — Left Click opens an orange portal, another Left Click a blue one; step into either to walk out of the other at full speed. Right Click cancels while aiming Talent points The single upgrade currency, earned through sorting XP, spent in the Skills tab Terminal The CRT computer at the counter — game lookup, play stats, store info Tidied / home An item sitting in its correct section, shelf, and row Base Stats Speed, Strength, Skill Haste and Insight. Each physical game copy's first matching shelf placement earns genre-based XP separately from skill points Store Progress The terminal's live item and fully tidied-title counts for the current store Steam Play History Your full consented local Steam library import and its available playtimes, including games outside the store No Record The scanner cannot identify the item; recognized games keep their local details even when online information is unavailable

docs.title: Modding
docs.text:
GameStart's store stock is data-driven, and the game has built-in, player-visible modding surfaces: packs, content pack files (.gspack), and the title bank.

Pre-release note: the pack formats are still evolving. Packs you make today may need updates as the game develops.

docs.title: Packs
docs.text:
A pack is a folder of content that changes what fills the store: exclude games from the shelves, rename the fictional titles, or restrict which platform sections a game may stock.

On the title menu's MODS screen you can:

  • See every installed pack (it says "No packs installed" until you add one).
  • Enable/disable each pack with its toggle.
  • See each pack's load order (#1, #2, …) — later packs win when two packs touch the same game.
  • Click "Open packs folder" to jump straight to where packs live on disk.

Packs now shape the night shift too: excluded games leave the pool the store stocks from, platform limits keep a game to its chosen sections, and fictional renames appear on box names. These changes decide which world a New Game builds — an existing save keeps the world it was made with, and its Continue will tell you if the pack set changed under it. Hiding games this way applies to the real titles; fictional titles can be renamed but not hidden.

docs.title: Installing a pack
docs.text:
1. On the title menu, open MODS and click "Open packs folder".
  2. Drop the pack's folder in there (one folder per pack).
  3. Back in the game, enable it with its toggle — it applies the next time you visit the store.

docs.title: Content packs (.gspack)
docs.text:
A content pack is a single .gspack file that can carry deeper, gameplay- shaping data — today that means skills and talents (the skills you unlock and the talent trees behind them), with more content kinds on the same road. Packs are data only: no code ever runs from a pack, and every pack is strictly validated on load — a broken pack is skipped with a message, never a crash.

To install one: drop the .gspack file into the Mods folder next to your saves (%USERPROFILE%\AppData\LocalLow\<studio>\<game>\Mods). Rename it to <name>.gspack.disabled to switch it off. Load order is alphabetical; a pack made with gameplay content stamps itself into your save, so a save made with mods will refuse to continue if the mod set changes (protecting the save, not punishing you — restore the packs and it loads again).

docs.title: The title bank
docs.text:
The fictional titles on the boxes come from word banks you can replace: create Mods\titlebank.json with your own words —

{
  "sp3aNames": ["My Favorite Fake Game"],
  "adjectives": ["Copperleaf", "Mossy"],
  "nouns": ["Harbor", "Junction"]
}

— and the store names its stock from your banks on the next launch. Real trademarks are refused (the whole file is skipped if any word matches the deny list), and a malformed file just falls back to the built-in names.

docs.title: Custom sounds
docs.text:
The store's sounds are swappable, one file per sound: drop 16-bit WAV files into Mods\audio\ named for the sound they replace —

pick.wav · place.wav · refuse.wav · complete.wav · chime.wav · footstep_a.wav · footstep_b.wav · ambient_loop.wav · kiosk_loop.wav

A file that isn't a plain 16-bit WAV is skipped with a note and the built-in sound keeps playing. Sounds are cosmetic — they never affect saves or playing together.

docs.title: Translations
docs.text: Content pack files can carry translations: a pack's language files replace any translated line of the game's text, and untranslated lines keep their English. Translations are cosmetic like sounds — installing one never affects a save. The game itself now ships Japanese, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese (Taiwan and Hong Kong), Spanish - Spain, Korean, Portuguese - Brazil, French, German — pick a language in Settings under GRAPHICS — and every line of the game's text is translatable, so a pack can polish a shipped language or start a brand-new one. The Hong Kong option is Standard Written Chinese with Hong Kong wording (網絡, 私隱, 地下 for the ground floor, 閣樓 for the mezzanine) on top of the Taiwan text — not colloquial Cantonese. Plural lines may carry .one, .few and .many variants; a pack that only fills .many still works.

docs.title: Steam Workshop
docs.text: The first slice of Workshop support is in the game: subscribe to a GameStart Workshop item and the game installs it on the next launch — .gspack files land in Mods, folder packs land on the MODS screen. Unsubscribe and it's removed the same way. (Publishing tools and the public Workshop hub go live with the Steam release — until then packs travel by file sharing, exactly as above.)

docs.title: Making a pack
docs.text:
The honest answer for now: the formats are documented for developers rather than polished for creators — a folder pack is a set of plain-text files, and a content pack currently needs the developer tools to build (a creator command-line tool is planned). If you're comfortable poking at files, see the Dev Glossary for where the technical documentation lives.

Packs and mods live only on the machine you installed them on: Steam Cloud, once enabled, carries your saves and not your mods.

docs.title: What packs can't touch
docs.text: Packs can curate which games appear in the store, but they cannot switch the Steam connection on for you. That choice always remains yours — see Privacy. Packs also can't run code, load DLLs, or reach outside their own data — by design.

docs.title: Privacy — the optional Steam connection
docs.text:
Planned for Steam-enabled builds. The secure connection remains unavailable in the current pre-release until its Steam setup and on-Steam checks are complete.

When available, GameStart can put your own Steam library on the store's shelves. This page is the plain-English record of exactly what that means. The short version: it is opt-in and read-only. Limited library details pass through GameStart's online library service and may be held there for up to six hours.

The service runs on Cloudflare's network. Processing and temporary storage may happen in places where Cloudflare operates its service. Before this connection is made available, this page will name the country or countries used for temporary storage.

The connection starts off. You can enable it from Settings → General → Privacy ("Use my Steam playtimes"); only your saved choice can turn it on. Installing or enabling a pack cannot connect Steam for you.

docs.title: What happens if you opt in
docs.text:
• The game asks the Steam app for a short-lived proof that you are signed in. It never asks for your Steam password.
  • GameStart's library service checks that proof with Steam, then requests your owned game titles, playtime totals, and last-played times. The service may temporarily keep your Steam account ID and your full owned-games list for no longer than six hours.
  • To prevent automated abuse, the service keeps a daily request counter for about 25 hours. That counter is not your connection address: it is a scrambled, one-way fingerprint of it, which cannot be turned back into an address.
  • The game downloads that limited list and fetches cover art onto your machine.
  • That data can fill the shelves, print the boxes, and show your personal Steam Play History in the terminal. That history covers your full imported library, including games absent from the store, and identifies the local account whose import it uses. Your choice takes effect at your next New Game — a night already in progress keeps the snapshot it was created with. Every New Game asks which catalog stocks the store, and MY GAMES + SHIPPED appears only while an import exists. While the connection is on, Settings also shows an Import Steam library button under the same row — press it to refresh your imported list and cover art.
  • Cover art is cached locally so later sessions load faster.
  • Store trailers are a separate switch under the same Settings row ("Play store trailers for my imported games"). We ask you when you turn Use my Steam playtimes on — a small card under that row offers Turn on or Not now (the same question follows the Import Steam library button when you press it); closing it without answering counts as Not now, and you can change the switch any time. During playtesting it may start on for players who use the Steam import and were never asked (Settings says so while that is the case); when on, the game downloads each store trailer from Steam once for your imported games (about 16 MB each), keeps them locally for up to 30 days, and deletes them when you turn it off. Turning it off is remembered — off always sticks — and the switch can also be turned off remotely. Turning Use my Steam playtimes off pauses store trailers (they need your Steam library), deletes the downloaded ones and resets that choice; turn playtimes back on and you are asked again.
  • Co-op: if you host a session, the resulting shelf entries (which games, and the playtime-based shelving unless you turned playtimes off) are shown to the players who join you, only while you host. Your sign-in proof and Steam password are never shared with them. Store trailers play on a guest's machine only if that guest turned them on.
  • Saves live on your machine and sync through Steam Cloud (just the save slots — never caches, your imported library, or consent choices), so a night can continue on another PC or the Steam Deck. Turn it off any time in the Steam client (game Properties → General → Steam Cloud).
  • Steam friends: hosting shows a joinable lobby to whoever your Room privacy choice allows, carrying only the session code, region, game version, your display name and the player count. Rich presence ("what I'm doing" in the friends list) is on by default and turns off in Settings → General. While you play through Steam, other players see your Steam persona name. Achievements and the two play counters (nights completed, co-op nights) live on your Steam profile, handled by Valve.

docs.title: What never happens
docs.text:
• Nothing from your library is bundled into the game — every player's store is prepared from the account that opted in.
  • The game cannot buy, sell, or modify anything on your Steam account.
  • Launch on an installed game's INFONET details page asks the Steam app on your computer to start that game. GameStart does not install it or change its Steam settings.
  • GameStart's publishing key is kept on the online service; it is not included in the game.

docs.title: If you opt out (or your profile is private)
docs.text: You get the fictional catalog — a full store of original parody games with authored facts. You can still scan recognized parody games and read their local profiles. Your personal Steam Play History stays unavailable without the required consent and matching local import. You can change your mind at any time; a new store uses the catalog you select for that New Game. Turning the connection off prevents new library requests. The service copy expires within six hours; locally cached cover art and the last downloaded list can remain until you clear the game's local data.

docs.title: Store Guide
docs.text: Your store is one big room with distinct sections. Learning the layout is the game — the better you know it, the faster every box finds its home.

docs.title: Finding your way
docs.text:
Three ways to get your bearings, all showing the same map:

  • Store map — hold Tab any time to raise a paper map of both floors. The red diamond is you; its notch points the way you're facing.
  • Store directory — the reading stand just inside the entrance, to your right as you walk in.
  • Wall map — mounted on the pier beside the front door.

The map colors match the marquee signs: each platform district fills in its band color, other sections in gray, the counter in red. Ramps are marked with arrows on both floor panels, and every color in the legend is paired with its printed name — you never have to rely on color alone.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
The store is now the two-floor layout: a big ground floor plus a mezzanine deck reached by two ramps — half the platform shelving lives upstairs.

  • Platform districts — every platform family owns a grouped district of wall bays: PayStation (blue) along the west, Newtondo (red) along the south, Vapor (black — the PC platform) in the north-west, and XRocks (green) in the north-east and east. Each district continues onto the mezzanine above it; the box shape gives every platform away (chunky cartridge boxes, slim jewel cases, tall keepcases, PC big boxes, little disc cases…). Colored marquee signs overhead mark each district.
  • Free shelves — the island gondolas in the middle of the floor (and a few on the deck): overflow space where any game box can live while you sort.
  • The counter — the heart of the store, under the north mezzanine strip: the register area and the terminal, a CRT computer where you can look up any game in the store and (if you connected Steam) your own play history. When nobody is using it, the screen drifts through a slow slideshow of cover art from the games stocked that night. Scan one of your imported Steam games with store trailers turned on in Settings and its trailer plays on the screen once before the game's details page. After the trailer, the details page shows Launch when you own that Steam game and it is installed. Click Launch or press L to start it. GameStart minimizes after the details page changes from Launching to Launched. If Steam rejects the request or the game cannot be detected, the page shows a launch error instead. Your co-op session stays connected. Friends see Playing and the Steam title above your character until you return to GameStart.
  • Wall posters — the tall portrait posters around the walls. Hold a game box and press E on one to put that game's poster there; if it is one of your imported Steam games and you turned on store trailers in Settings, its trailer plays on the poster instead (the prompt tells you which: "hang … poster" or "play … trailer here"). While the store makes the new poster, a short "Hanging…" line shows along the poster's bottom edge and the old poster stays up; the new one appears when it is ready. The first time you play a game's trailer the store has to fetch it: the poster shows that game's cover with a progress line along the bottom edge, then the trailer starts on its own. Everyone in a co-op store sees the same game on each poster; the trailer itself plays only for players who turned store trailers on. While a poster plays a trailer, a small line along its bottom edge reminds you that trailers belong to their publishers and are played from Steam for games you own.
  • TV screens — the wall-mounted TVs (and the small sets on some shelves). Left alone, a TV drifts through the same cover-art slideshow as the terminal, and — if you turned on store trailers in Settings — plays the trailers of your imported Steam games that the store has already fetched, one after another, on whichever TVs you are looking at. Hold a game box and press E on a TV to put that game on it: its trailer if it can play here, otherwise its cover (the prompt tells you which: "play … trailer here" or "show … cover here"). A trailer the store has not fetched yet starts as that game's cover with a progress line along the bottom edge, and begins playing when it is ready. Everyone in a co-op store sees the same game on that TV, the trailer itself plays only for players who turned store trailers on, and a TV you set keeps your game (instead of the slideshow and the store's own trailers) until the store closes. The same small line about publishers appears along a TV's bottom edge while it plays a trailer.
  • Trailer options (hold E) — on a screen that is playing a trailer (a poster, a TV or the terminal), hold E (or hold the gamepad's A button) for about half a second to open a small wheel of choices: Mute / Unmute that one screen, Stop the trailer (a poster goes back to the game's poster; a TV goes back to the game's cover, or to its slideshow if the store put that trailer on; the terminal goes back to the game's details page), and — with a game box in hand — the usual Play trailer / Hang poster (on a TV: Show cover). Move the mouse (or the right stick) toward a choice and let go of E to pick it; letting go with nothing chosen does what a tap would have done; right-click (or the throw button) cancels. A quick tap of E on those screens still does what it always did. A screen that is still fetching a trailer offers Stop on its own — that leaves the game's cover up and stops waiting for the trailer. Muting one screen is just for you; stopping a trailer that a player put on a poster is seen by everyone in a co-op store (the store's own default trailers, and the terminal's, stop just for you). There is also a Mute trailer sound switch in Settings > Audio that silences every trailer at once, and trailer sound follows the Ambience Volume slider.
  • Hardware & gear — the console-accessory wall on the east side stocks the console boxes (every platform and generation) alongside the peripherals; these keep their own homes off the game shelves.

docs.title: Handling a game
docs.text:
Picking one up and shelving one both have a bit of give to them:

  • Picking up — the game comes in steady, then gives a short buzz as it lands in your hands. It is yours from the moment you press the key; the shake is only what the game does on arrival, so nothing waits on it. Only the game you just picked up shakes — the ones already in your hands stay put.
  • Shelving — a game settles once it reaches its slot: a small nudge and tilt that fades out. It comes out slightly different every time, so filling a row one box at a time does not look like the same animation on repeat. The settle is only for show — the game counts as shelved the moment it reaches the slot, so anything that happens on a placement happens on time.

Neither one changes what a game does, only how it looks doing it.

docs.title: Reading a game box
docs.text:
The box itself tells you a lot:

  • Front: cover art, platform styling, title.
  • Back: publisher blurb, screenshots, and feature bullets — and, if you connected Steam, a shelf label with your logged hours and the year you last booted the game. Hold F to inspect a box up close; release F to lower it smoothly back into your hand.
  • Planned: the exact numbers move off the box into the terminal, replaced by a fuzzy staff-pick badge that only hints at playtime — never exact numbers.

docs.title: Statistics and scanning
docs.text:
The terminal's Statistics page separates Store Progress from Steam Play History. Store progress follows the current tidying count; taking a correctly placed box back off its shelf can reduce it. Titles fully tidied counts a game only once all of its required copies are tidied, including copies in different box versions.

Steam Play History uses your full locally imported library when you have consented, including games that are not in the store. The page identifies whose history it is and when it was imported. Unknown playtime is shown as unavailable, not as zero.

Scanning a recognized game or parody shows its available local facts even offline. An online lookup failure keeps those facts visible; No Record is for an item the scanner cannot identify. A missing cover has its own placeholder. The handheld Pip-Boy readout stays on the game you scanned while the store remains live.

docs.title: Section signs & grand opening
docs.text:
Each section has an overhead sign. Planned: a fully tidied section's sign lights up and stays lit. The store is ready for its grand opening when its required homes are filled. The OPEN sign at the front door lets you decide when to open; in co-op, only the host can activate it.

The GRAND OPENING report records Items tidied, Titles fully tidied, Lifetime sorting XP, Time to grand opening, Fixtures full and Sections done. Learned skills appear when there are names to show. Roll Credits plays the credits; finishing or skipping that first roll returns to the report.

Later, Continue revisits the completed store with normal handling and skills. The host can use the OPEN sign to replay the credits; that replay finishes at Title. Later tidying does not rewrite the original report or first-completion time.

docs.title: Genre dividers (dev-flag preview)
docs.text: With the shelf-composer dev flag enabled, the shelves show which genre they want in the style of record-store genre dividers: a colored rail runs along the shelf edge for the whole stretch that wants one genre, with a raised divider tab carrying the genre's name (ACTION, RPG, STRATEGY…) at the start of the stretch and a small matching tab closing its end. Neighboring slots on a shelf row that want the same genre share one divider group — each row of an Action bay on the PayStation wall reads as one named stretch, so every shelf row carries its own name tab along with its colored rail. Shelves open to anything wear a neutral gray divider tab reading Discount or Sale. Each genre keeps its own distinct color everywhere in the store, and the name is always printed on the tab, so you never have to rely on color alone. The dividers are guidance only: they never block items, and they only appear on boots where the composer's plan is active.

docs.title: Talents & Gear
docs.text: Talents are live end to end: earn talent points, spend them in the pause menu's Skills tab, and cast skills with keys 1–6.

docs.title: Talent points
docs.text: Talent points buy skill upgrades. Regular tidying earns sorting XP, which converts into talent points as you progress.

docs.title: Base Stats
docs.text:
The separate Base Stats tab shows Speed, Strength, Skill Haste and Insight. You can also press B to open these details while in the store. Press the same control again, press Esc, or choose Back to close them. Rebinding the shortcut changes both opening and closing it.

Each individual game copy earns genre-based Base Stats XP the first time you put that copy on a matching shelf. Moving the same copy out and back does not earn it again. This is separate from sorting XP and the points you spend on skills.

docs.title: The Skills tab
docs.text:
Open the pause menu and pick Skills to spend talents:

  • Your unspent talent points show at the top.
  • Your skills sit on the left as a row of icon tiles, in skill-bar order, each with its key badge and level (like Lv 2/10). Click a tile — or move to it with the stick — and its details fill the right side: what it does, which key uses it, and every number one per line as now → next (like Cooldown (s): 60 → 55), so you can see exactly what the upgrade changes.
  • A dot in a tile's corner means there is a level to buy: bright when you can afford it right now, dim when you still need points. The Skills tab itself shows a dot while anything is affordable. The right side spells the dot out — Upgradeable now, or how many points you are short.
  • Levels get pricier as you climb: level 1 costs 3 talent points, level 2 5, level 3 7, and so on (two more each level). The Upgrade button on the right always shows the exact price; press it to buy the next level. On a controller, A on the highlighted skill buys it straight away. A maxed skill says MAX.

docs.title: In After-Hours Co-op
docs.text: Talent points are the team's — one shared pot everyone earns into. Any player can press Upgrade: the points come out of that shared pot, and every player in the session gets the new level. Skills themselves stay your own — you cast on your own cooldowns, and buying a level never starts anyone else's.

docs.title: The skill bar (keys 1–6)
docs.text:
The skill bar always keeps six positions. Press keyboard keys 1–6 to cast. (The skill keys are keyboard-only for now — no gamepad binding yet.)

  • Unused positions say empty, unavailable skills say locked, and learned skills show their level.
  • A cast only "spends" the skill when it actually does something. If it can't work right now, a short hint pops up instead — like "Hold a box first", "On cooldown", or "No charges left" — and no cooldown starts.
  • Cooldowns refill on their own; higher levels mostly shorten them.

docs.title: Active skills
docs.text:
Key Skill What it does 1 Shelf Guide Highlights the shelf where the box in your hands belongs — a crystal flies from in front of you to the shelf board the box belongs on, and that board's slots glow through walls while you still hold that box; higher levels cut the cooldown 2 Scope Shot Hold a game and scope in: the view narrows to a circular scope and steadies. One shot — into an empty slot the game fits, it flies there in a straight line and settles in; anywhere else, it leaves your hands along the line of the shot. If that line ends in a pile of games on the floor, it hits with weight — the game drops where it struck and ploughs a lane through the pile, while anything already shelved stays put. C cycles the two magnifications while scoped. Press 2 again (or right-click) to back out for free 3 Pip-Boy Opens a large INFONET readout for the box you're holding. You can keep moving and handling boxes, but other skills wait; press 3 or Esc to close it. Dropping or throwing the scanned box also closes it. If the box is a Steam game you own and have installed, the readout offers [L] LAUNCH ON STEAM — press L to start it through Steam 4 Tendril Grab Reels copies of the game you're holding in from across your district — shelf fronts and loose strays alike — straight into your hands, up to eight a cast. Level 2 reaches the districts next to you as well; level 3 digs behind the front copy; level 4 pulls from anywhere in the store and brings the whole catch in at once instead of one at a time 5 Bubble Carry Seals the box in your hands inside a bubble that floats it to its home shelf on its own — your hands stay free. If that home is full, the bubble tries the next home for the same game; if every home is full, it pops and the box settles nearby 6 Portal Pistol Arm it, then Left Click a wall or the floor to open the orange portal and Left Click again for the blue one — step into either and you walk out of the other, keeping your speed. Right Click cancels while you're aiming; the pair fades on its own after about half a minute

Portal Return (the link-a-pad-to-a-shelf return gadget) has clocked out of the skill bar for now — it may return in a later store phase.

docs.title: Passive skills
docs.text:
Passives work all the time once learned — no key, no cooldown:

Skill What it does Deluxe Cart Carry more boxes at once — two levels, each raising your carry limit further Plumbob Guide While you hold a box, a hovering gem marks the shelf where it belongs Stock Sense While you hold a box, nearby copies of the same game get a purple outline — the "reunite the stack" glow

A note on the glow: highlighting matching games used to be free for everyone. It now belongs to Stock Sense — if you liked it, it's a cheap early buy.

docs.title: The retired gadget shelf
docs.text: Gadgets were physical store gear — each a loving parody of infamous game-industry hardware. The classic shelf has since retired, its powers grown up and shipped as proper skills: the Sorter's Magnet's grab lives on in Tendril Grab, the Deluxe Pack ships as the Deluxe Cart passive, and the Pocket Terminal's database stays where it always lived — the counter terminal. The Spotter Visor came back in person for a while — its scanner vision first split into the Pip-Boy skill and the Stock Sense glow, then the visor itself returned to the bar — but key 2 now belongs to Scope Shot, and the visor is off the bar again. Its talent branch is still there if it ever comes back. The Buddy clocked out with the rest of the classic shelf. New gadgets may arrive with later store phases.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
Pick up → find the right spot → place → watch the store come together. Every copy of a game has a proper home: the right section, the right shelf, the right row. When you hold a box near shelving, a ghost preview shows exactly where it would sit — and once you've learned the Stock Sense skill (Talents & Gear), other copies of the same game glow so you can reunite the stack.

Neaten a row anytime with Face (F) — pulling boxes forward into a tidy front line, just like real shelf work.

docs.title: Price tags
docs.text:
Every row of games on a shelf has a price tag on the rail under it. Empty shelves have no tag.

  • White tag — those copies are in the right home, and every copy of that game is now on the shelves this game has claimed. The run is finished. A game the night split across two stacks turns white on BOTH once the pair holds all its copies — it does not have to fit them into one shelf.
  • Plain tag — the copies are in the right home, but not every copy of that game is home yet: more are still out on the floor, in a basket, or in your hands. Keep going; the tag turns white when the game's own shelves hold the whole run.
  • Yellow border — when a game already has a chosen home somewhere else tonight, or a stack cannot hold the copies one planned stack should hold, or it is sitting in more stacks than the night planned, EVERY tag of that game picks up a thick yellow border — the finished white home stack included — so you can see at a glance which game needs consolidating. If the night planned two stacks of four for an eight-copy game, two right-home stacks stay clean; a stack that cannot hold four, or a third stack, lights the border up for the whole game. Consolidate the extras away and the borders go with them.
  • Red tag — something in that run is in the wrong section.

If you place a box in a spot that fits but is the wrong section, the tag goes red on the spot — that's the store telling you "close, but no." No penalty, no timer; it just stays red until you make it right. A right-home stack that does not yet hold every copy of that game stays a plain tag, never white, never red — as long as it is one of the stacks the night planned and can hold that stack's share. Past either, that game's tags pick up the yellow border.

docs.title: One game, one home for the night
docs.text:
The first run where you correctly shelf a game becomes that game's chosen home for the night.

  • More copies placed in that run keep the right-home tag. It turns white when every copy of that game is on that shelf.
  • Copies placed in another regular run light the yellow border up on that game's tags, even when that section would normally suit the game — unless those extra stacks are still inside the night's planned seat count. A stack that cannot hold the planned copies per stack, or stacks beyond that count, light it up too.
  • The choice resets only after every copy of that game has been removed from regular shelves. The next correct placement chooses a new home.
  • Shelving skills use the chosen run too. If it cannot take another box, they wait instead of sending the box to a run that would show red.

docs.title: Finishing the night
docs.text:
Tidying makes the store ready; you decide when it opens. Once the store's required homes are filled, the OPEN/CLOSED sign by the front door can open the store. The current HUD percentage describes live tidiness; it does not automatically start the ending.

Walk over and flip the sign to OPEN when ready. The first completion records a GRAND OPENING report and offers the credits. In co-op, only the host opens the store, while each player can finish or skip their own credits independently.

Continue a completed save to revisit it with normal movement, handling and skills. The host can deliberately replay the ending through the sign; that credit replay returns to Title. The original report and time remain unchanged.

Planned: when the last copy of a game is correctly shelved, that stack gets a persistent gleam — a little "done ✓" the store remembers. Finishing a section will also light its overhead sign.

docs.title: XP
docs.text: Correct placements earn XP (you'll see the +XP pop). XP raises your clerk level. There is no money in the store — your reward currency is talent points (Talents & Gear).
